title: Not Part of the Garden
aliases: Found While Looking For Something Else
logline: A garden made over half a century on an old cinnamon and rubber estate, where hills were moved, terraces cut and a whole view cleared in a few hours, and whose most important view ends on something the garden has never owned: the white dome of a temple on the far side of the water. The record keeps two kinds of reaching side by side, attempts to buy the land next door that did not succeed, and views opened onto land and buildings nobody bought. The film is one unbroken walk in the way the garden was made to be entered, and it stops where the garden was made to stop.
human_question: When I want to look at something I will never own, what exactly am I taking, and is that wanting the same as the wanting to have it?

place.what_kind_of_place: A designed landscape garden of about twenty-five acres laid over two low hills on a promontory in a brackish lake, a mile inland from the open sea. It was a cinnamon garden under the Dutch and a rubber estate under the British; from the late 1940s one man remade it for the rest of his life into a sequence of enclosed spaces and long cut vistas: terraces, a buried estate road that became a sunken ditch, a water meadow of rice squares, pavilions, stairs cut into a cliff, and sculpture placed as a pointer or a stopping-place. It is not a garden of flowers. It is green on green, light and shade, and views. The main view, from the terrace in front of the old bungalow, runs south over a lawn and down over a small hill with a large pot and a leaning tree on its top, across a thin sliver of lake, to the white dome of a Buddhist temple on the far shore. The garden does not own the temple; its main view is composed out of things beyond its own boundary. The estate is now held by a trust, visited on guided tours, and part of it is let to overnight guests.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Because the garden itself stages a reveal, and the film only has to walk into it. The approach is designed to be blind: a track through paddy to a wooded hill, an overgrown gateway, a steep drive swinging up through trees in shade, and a cascade of steps; only at the top of the steps, on the terrace, does the whole composition open at once, a lawn falling away, a pot under a tree on a hill, a line of water, and one white point on the far side. The biographer who described it compared the moment to having a blindfold taken off. With the sound off it is a complete piece: dark to light, climbing to arriving, enclosure to distance, and then a long stillness in front of a view that looks painted and is not.
place.what_moves_or_changes: The camera moves once, continuously, and then stops; nothing else in the film is under the crew's control. Morning light comes in from the east and slides across the lawn and the side of the far dome; mist, when there is any, lifts off the lake; leaves come down, birds cross the vista, a boat may pass on the water. If the garden is being swept or cut that morning, as a garden of this kind has to be almost daily, the sound of it is in the track and the work is seen only as tools and fallen leaf, never as faces. The single real change the film waits for is the light on the dome: in the first hour it goes from grey to white.
place.when_it_looks_best: The drier months on this coast, roughly December to March, before the south-west monsoon; clear air after overnight rain makes the far shore read sharply, and a still morning can hold a low mist on the lake. Within the day, from about half past six to half past eight in the morning: the sun is low in the east, the drive is still in deep shade so the reveal at the top of the steps is a real change of exposure, the dome takes side light, and the public garden tours, which begin later in the morning, have not started. Treatment, and how it differs from every other film in the group: one unbroken take, stabilised, at standing eye height, on a 35 mm lens, walking the designed approach from the gate to the terrace and then stopping to hold the main view for about ninety seconds with no push-in and no zoom. No drone, no long lens, no cut, no interior. The camera never crosses the water and never walks down the view towards the hill or the dome. Sound is live only: footsteps on laterite and stone, birds, leaves, the lake. The payoff is the stop itself: the dome sits small and white in a normal field of view, a few per cent of the frame, and the film ends without going any closer to it.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A walk into a famous garden at first light, made as one continuous shot. Shade, a gateway gone over to creepers, a steep drive, steps, and then, all at once, sun and space: a lawn, a hill with a pot and a leaning tree, a strip of water, and far off a white dome. The camera stops and looks for a minute and a half while the light comes up on it. It resolves on its own terms, closed to open, climb to arrival, and it is the only film in its group that never cuts.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The voice turns the walk into a demonstration of the one factor the group most needs kept apart from greed. The texts say the wish to do is the wish to take up an object and is not the force that makes the mind stick to it, a wanting without the sticking. This garden's written record holds two kinds of reaching side by side: attempts to buy neighbouring land that did not succeed, and views made onto water, land and a dome that nobody bought. The record gives the acts and cannot give the minds, and the film says so rather than choosing. Then the second concept: every mind takes an object and tastes it, and the feeling varies with the object; nothing in that sentence requires owning what is tasted. The walk ends at the edge of what was bought, facing what was not, and the camera does not go any closer. Nobody is shown or said to be wanting anything.

sequence.on_screen: The take begins in shade at the boundary of the estate: a laterite track ending at an overgrown gateway in a wall of trees. The camera walks through it at eye height, without cutting, onto the foot of a steep drive that swings up and away under the canopy. Birds, footsteps, nothing else.
sequence.voice: In 1948, or 1949, since the two years are both in print, a young lawyer named Geoffrey Bawa bought an old estate here: rubber, and before the rubber, cinnamon. He spent the next half century turning it into what this camera is walking into. The camera is going to come in the way the garden was made to be entered, and stop where it was made to stop. It will not cut.

sequence.on_screen: Still one take: up the drive in near darkness, roots and stones in the laterite, the light only in flecks on the ground. On the left, glimpses of a sunken ditch where an old road ran. The pace is slow and even; the camera does not look up yet.
sequence.voice: His biographer wrote that since 1948 hills have been moved here, terraces cut, woods replanted and the old estate road buried in a ditch. He also wrote what happens if the work stops: in a week the paths clog with leaves; in a month the lawns run wild; in two or three years the jungle is back. The texts in this series name a factor they call the wish to do. One of them says it is the wish to take up an object, and that it is not the force that makes the mind stick to that object. The sticking has other names: greed, craving, longing.

sequence.on_screen: The drive levels out at the foot of a cascade of steps. The camera begins to climb them, still without a cut. Above, the canopy thins; the top step is a bright line against the sky.
sequence.voice: In 1959 a colleague, the architect Ulrik Plesner, wrote down a few hours' work here. While a hill was being dug and stairs finished, it was realised that a view lay hidden behind two hundred metres of trees. The chairs were turned, all other work was abandoned, and in a few hours the trees were down and a whole new view was made. The Margaya names the factor that carries the mind onto an object, and says that the effort to bring the mind to places it has not yet reached, to know what it did not know, is what people call thinking.

sequence.on_screen: Near the top of the steps. The frame is filled with the last risers and the edge of the terrace, bright; the view is not yet visible. The camera slows almost to a stop.
sequence.voice: The same biographer records two other acts, without exact dates. Attempts to buy the lower half of the promontory did not succeed; two neighbouring islands in the lake were bought. Later, the owner of the land to the west would not sell. What was built instead, on that side, was a loggia framing a view towards the land that was not sold. The record gives the acts. It does not give, and no record could give, the mind they were done with. The Margaya says the wish to do looks a little like greed but has none of greed's sticking: it is a wanting without the sticking. In a mind that goes with greed, it goes with greed. In a mind against greed, it goes against it.

sequence.on_screen: The camera reaches the terrace and turns, and the garden opens at once: sun, a lawn falling away, a corridor of trees, a small hill with a large pot and a single leaning tree on top, a thin bright line of lake beyond it, and past the water, small and white, the dome of a temple on the far shore. The walk stops. The frame is held at 35 mm, level, no push-in.
sequence.voice: This is what the whole approach was built to arrive at. The last thing in it is not part of the garden. The dome belongs to a temple across the water. The garden has never owned it, and its most important view ends on it. The maker wrote that the ground here was about twenty-five acres, but that with the lakes around it, the land beyond seems to go on forever.

sequence.on_screen: The hold continues. The low sun moves onto the side of the dome and it turns from grey to white; a bird crosses the vista; a leaf comes down on the lawn in the foreground. Nothing else moves. Live sound only.
sequence.voice: The texts say that every mind takes an object, and that with every mind comes feeling, which tastes the flavour of that object; and since objects are of many kinds, the feeling differs with them. Nothing in that sentence asks who the object belongs to. What the eye takes from here is an object, and only an object.

sequence.on_screen: Still held. The whole composition, pot, tree, water and dome, in full morning light. The camera does not move any closer, then or at the end; the film ends on the held frame, and the sound runs a few seconds past the picture.
sequence.voice: Of the kinds of mind the texts count with pleasant feeling, all but one have it as gladness in the mind, not in the body, and there are sixty-two of those: four of them rooted in greed, two without roots, twelve counted beautiful, and forty-four in the states of deep concentration. So gladness at a view is counted on both sides, and the count does not say which side any one morning's gladness is on. The camera cannot say either. The texts add that the wish to do, turned against greed and developed, carries a mind to its highest aims. That cannot be filmed. The film can only stop here, at the edge of what was bought, facing what was not.

concept_merge.why_together: C021 is the primary and carries five of the seven beats. Of its six occasional factors the film uses two and leaves the rest alone. Desire-to-act is the centre: the Pradeepika defines it as the wish to take up the object and says it is not the force that makes the mind stick to it, the sticking being called greed, craving and longing [C021-P:L69]; the Margaya calls it the wish to do, says it resembles greed a little but lacks greed's sticking, a wanting without sticking, and that it accords with greed in greed-accompanied minds and opposes greed in minds opposed to it [C021-M:L27]. Initial application enters once, on a documented moment of finding: the Margaya says the effort to bring the mind to places it has not reached, to know what it did not know, is what is called thinking [C021-M:L7]. C032 is supporting and enters only when the view does. The Pradeepika says every mind takes an object and so every mind has feeling, the power of tasting the object's flavour, which varies with the object [C032-P:L43]; the Margaya's count puts the joyful minds in sixty-two, four of them greed-rooted and the rest wholesome sense-sphere, rootless and absorption minds [C032-M:L9], while bodily pleasure has a single seat in touch [C032-M:L7].
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the object of a wish and the possession of a thing are different items, and that a place can be built almost entirely out of the first. C021 alone would make a film about drive, which the group already has twice (the shooting-ground film and the pilgrimage-shrine film). C032 alone would make a film about the pleasure of a view, which would slide towards 'chase good vibes', a reading its digest refuses. Together they say something neither says alone: the wish takes up an object, the feeling tastes the object, and neither needs to own it; the sticking is a third thing, and neither the record of this garden nor the camera can show where it was present. The garden's own written history is the evidence, because it keeps the two kinds of reaching, buying land and making views, side by side and leaves the minds out.

concept_links.why: The digest's central finding for this group is that wanting to do is not the same as clinging: the Pradeepika's desire-to-act is the wish to take up the object and not the force that makes the mind stick to it, the sticking being named greed, craving and longing, and the wish itself takes the object without regard to whether it is good or bad [C021-P:L69]; the Margaya's wish to do resembles greed a little but has no sticking, and it accords with greed in greed-accompanied minds and opposes greed in minds opposed to it [C021-M:L27]; developed, it helps suppress craving and leads towards absorption and liberation [C021-P:L75]. This garden's documented history is where that distinction is the only honest reading of the record, because the record holds two kinds of act about the same ground: attempts to buy neighbouring land that did not succeed, and views composed onto land, water and a temple dome that were never bought, the main vista ending on something that belongs to someone else. The film uses the distinction without assigning it: it never says which mind any act was done with, and it says why (the record gives acts, not minds). Initial application is used once, on the one eyewitness moment the record contains, the view found behind two hundred metres of trees in 1959; the Margaya's words are that the effort to bring the mind where it has not reached, to know what it did not know, is called thinking [C021-M:L7]. The digest's does_not_transfer lines bind the voice: fifty years of work is never called virtuous ('hard work is always virtuous' is refused; the physical labour on screen is not the mental factor of effort, which the film does not claim to show); the maker's passion is never offered as a guarantee ('follow your passion' is refused); and desire is never made the enemy, since the source says the opposite about desire-to-act. Decision, effort, rapture and the boat-and-hill image are left to the group's other films.

Feeling enters when the view does, and only to make one point the view can carry honestly: the Pradeepika says every mind arises taking an object, so feeling, the power of tasting the object's flavour, is present in every mind, and it varies with the kind of object [C032-P:L43]. Tasting an object needs the object, not the ownership of it, which is the whole situation of a view that ends on a neighbour's temple. The Margaya's count is used to refuse a verdict rather than to make one: sixty-two minds carry mental joy, four of them greed-rooted, twelve beautiful sense-sphere minds and the rest rootless and absorption minds [C032-M:L9], and bodily pleasure has one seat only, touch [C032-M:L7], so the gladness a view gives is mental and the count places it in both wholesome and unwholesome minds without saying which. The digest's does_not_transfer lines bind it: the film does not offer pleasant feeling as a goal ('chase good vibes' is refused), does not make pleasure the enemy or the place where wanting begins (the group gloss is editorial, as the digest says), and does not treat the neutral as numb. The Pradeepika's teaching that even pleasant feeling is suffering in the sense of rise and fall and of change [C032-P:L115] [C032-P:L117] is deliberately not used: the group's hill-station film carries it, and here it would turn a view into a sermon.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That wanting to look at something and wanting to have it are two different things, and that a place can be made almost entirely out of the first. The proof is on screen and needs no belief: the most important view of a famous private garden ends on a white dome across the water that the garden has never owned, and the camera, having walked all the way there, stops and does not go any closer. What the viewer is not told is which mind anyone had; the film says plainly that the record cannot tell it.
what_must_be_real: The approach, the terrace and the view exactly as the garden now has them; nothing moved, trimmed, dressed or lit for the camera. The dome is filmed only from inside the garden, at a normal focal length, at whatever size it actually appears; it is never brought closer by a long lens, a crop or a drone, and the temple is never visited, filmed at close range or identified in the prose. The one take is one take: no hidden cut, no stitched move. If the garden's own staff are sweeping or cutting that morning they are not directed or asked to perform, and are seen, if at all, as tools, hands and fallen leaf, never as faces. No overnight guest or tour visitor is in frame. Every historical statement in the voice is one the record actually makes, with its date or its lack of one; the quotations from the biographer, the colleague and the maker are quoted as their words, not as facts about anyone's mind.
position_hint: Late in GRP-02, after the films that establish what greed is and how its dials work, and after the shooting-ground film has said that drive has no colour of its own. This is the group's release: the one film whose subject is wanting that is not sticking, and whose last shot is a wanting that takes an object and holds nothing. It should not sit next to the shooting-ground film, which shares its primary concept.
risks: Biography. The garden is one man's life's work and every source about it is about him; decision 1 forbids a film about a person's life. The voice names him in two beats, for dated acts and one sentence he wrote about the land, and otherwise speaks of the garden and its record.

A person in a mental state. The group's floor is that no identifiable person is shown or narrated as wanting. The sources are full of attributions ('ambitions to buy out his neighbour', 'derived so much pleasure', 'dreamt of making a garden'); none of them enters the voice. The voice gives acts (bought, tried to buy, built, cleared) and quotes statements about the land, and it says outright that the record does not give the mind.

The temple's community as an exhibit, or the view as an ownership question. The temple is never filmed except as the dome at the size the garden's view gives it; no monk, devotee, ceremony or temple sound is used; the temple is never named in the prose. The biographer's anecdote of a request from the temple for a contribution to repainting the dome, and the answer given, is recorded in the historical thread and deliberately kept out of the voice: it would put a price and a request on the view, invite a reading of two named people's minds, and could read as mocking either party.

Remembrance register. The small hill in the middle of the main view is where the maker's ashes were scattered in 2003 (published garden writing and one Commons file description say so). The film does not mention it, does not walk towards the hill, frames no marker, and the payoff is about the dome beyond the hill, not the hill. His illness in his last years, which the biographer describes, is not used.

Entering a live question about the trust or the hotel. The biographer asked in 2002 whether such a place should be frozen and preserved or let go back to jungle; the estate is now kept by a trust with paid tours and guest rooms. The film does not quote that question, does not comment on how the estate is run now, and does not name any current operator.

The neighbouring land. The neighbour who declined to sell is referred to only as 'the owner', undated as the record leaves them; no neighbouring house, field or person is filmed as such, and the loggia facing that land is mentioned, not shown, because it lies within guest accommodation.

Collision with a GRP-03 country-house film. The Richmond Castle proposal for IDEA-0043 (a private estate in trust, filmed as one continuous move) was refused on 2026-09-26 and the slot reopened; if it is refilled with another private estate or a single-take film, this film's treatment must be checked against it.

Collision in the district. The Island Hermitage lake-island proposal for IDEA-0036 (same district, looking across water at something never reached) was refused on 2026-09-26 and the slot reopened; if a Galle District film replaces it, check it against this one's view across water.

Analogy creep. The film must not become 'the garden is like the mind'. The record is the evidence: dated acts of buying and of view-making, and a view that ends on property that is not the garden's. If a beat only works as a resemblance, it is cut.

The one-take treatment can fail on the day (a guest on the terrace, a gardener in frame without consent, a stumble on the steps). The film is shot on several mornings and the best complete take is used; a cut is not an acceptable repair.
drop_if: The white dome is not in fact visible from the entrance terrace today (trees grown up, a building put up in the gap), since the payoff is that sight and the biographer's description of it is from 2002.
The trust will not permit an early-morning continuous take of the approach and the terrace without guests or staff directed out of the way.
The only way to make the payoff read is to bring the dome closer by lens or drone, which would contradict the film.

The acquisition attempts and the loggia prove, on checking the 1990 book or the biographer's later garden monograph, to be misreported; the C021 argument rests on the record holding both kinds of act.

connections.note: The group's other C021-primary film (written): a former shooting reserve that has become the most watched wild ground on the island, where the texts' claim is that the six occasional factors have no colour of their own and the same stalk served two laws. That film is about drive under any aim, filmed from a halted vehicle with an 800 mm lens. This one takes a narrower point from the same concept, that the wish to do takes up an object and is not the sticking, and is filmed walking, on a 35 mm lens, never on a long lens. The two do not share a voice line; this one leaves effort and the colourless-factors sentence to that film.

The group's pilgrimage-shrine film (written) closes on the same C021 finding from the side of a vow to build and uses the decision factor on a colonial footnote. This film uses neither decision nor building as its subject: its evidence is a record of views made onto things not owned. Noon, locked frames and a straight-down drone there; early morning, one walking take and no drone here.

The group's hill-station film (written) uses C032 through the body: bodily pleasure's single seat in touch, a whole town built for cool air, and the suffering of change as frost melting. This film uses C032 through an object: the feeling that tastes an object comes with taking it, and nearly all counted pleasure is mental, so a view's gladness is counted on both sides. Locked macro and wides at a frozen dawn there; a walking 35 mm take in warm morning light here. Neither film uses the other's C032 lines as its point.

selection.reason: Kept on the blind GRP-02 selection's proposal, after testing both halves and replacing the story the proposal rested on. The proposal's binding facts were 'it is said' garden writing: that a hill was lowered and a lane sunk so as not to interrupt the view of the temple. Those claims were traced and remain unconfirmed in any primary reached (one garden blog says three metres were taken off a hilltop to open a glimpse of water and a stupa; another says it was so the view down to the lake would not be interrupted; the biographer says only that hills were moved and the old road buried in a ha-ha). What the biographer's full account of the garden (David Robson, 2002, reached through its reproduction on Archnet) does document is better for the concept: failed attempts to buy neighbouring land, a loggia then built to frame a view of the land that was not sold, a main vista that ends on a temple dome the garden does not own, and an eyewitness account from 1959 of a hidden view found and cleared in a few hours. That record keeps having and viewing side by side, which is C021's own distinction between the wish to do and the sticking. The place half needed no argument. The film's weaknesses are stated in the review note.

review.note: This record's body was replaced in full on 2026-09-26 in the blind GRP-02 re-selection, written without reading the previous body. The previous status was already pending, so no confirmation or rejection has been reset, but under standing decision 9 any earlier reading of this record no longer applies. The concepts are unchanged (C021 primary, C032 supporting). The location, proposed by Claude, is a designed landscape garden on a lake a mile inland of the south-west coast, which was the blind selection's proposal; it was tested, its story was rebuilt on a better source, and it was kept. Corrections to the proposal and to its sources: (1) the district is the one named in suggested_location.region, not the province Wikipedia gives: OpenStreetMap/Nominatim puts the estate there, it lies south of the river that divides the two districts, and its Divisional Secretariat belongs to that district; (2) the proposal's 'rented from 1948 and bought in 1949 by the architect' is not what its source says: Wikipedia says the bungalow was let in 1948 to a local tax collector and bought by him in 1949, while the biographer and the trust both give 1948; both dates are kept; (3) the proposal's 'reworked it for forty years' is wrong on its own dates (the biographer says more than half a century, 1948 to 2003); (4) the lowered hill and sunk lane are not in the biographer's text: he says the estate road was buried in a ha-ha and that 'hills have been moved', and the three-metre figure appears only in later garden writing, told two ways; (5) the anecdote that the temple 'later heard its stupa was the focus of the vista' is the biographer's, and it continues with a request for money to repaint the dome and an offer of half the cost because only half could be seen; it is recorded but kept out of the voice. The film's story now rests on the biographer's account of failed attempts to buy neighbouring land and of a loggia built to frame the view of land not sold, on a 1959 eyewitness account of a hidden view cleared in a few hours (quoted by a 1986 monograph), and on the maker's own sentence about the land beyond seeming to go on forever. Please judge in particular: whether a single man's garden can be filmed without becoming his biography; whether this and the proposed GRP-03 country-house film (IDEA-0043) are too close as private estates now held in trust; and whether this and the proposed GRP-03 lake-island film (IDEA-0036) are too close as two films in one district looking across a lake. The district count for the location's district (named in suggested_location.region) moves from 4 to 5, and to 6 if the GRP-03 lake-island film is kept. Audit 2026-09-26: independent second check. Changed: (1) beat 3 said Plesner recorded 'one morning's work'; his quoted text (Robson 2002, from Taylor 1986) says 'in a few hours', with no time of day; corrected. (2) Beat 4 gave only the failed purchases; Robson's same sentence continues 'but he did manage to acquire two neighbouring islands'. Told halfway, it tilted the record toward the film's thesis; the voice now includes the islands. (3) Beat 7 said 'of the pleasant feelings the texts count, all but one are gladness'; the count (C032-M:L7, L9) is of kinds of mind: 63 with pleasant feeling, 62 of them mental; reworded. (4) Connections to IDEA-0043 (Richmond Castle) and IDEA-0036 (Island Hermitage) removed and the matching risks, position_hint, region and research_note updated, because both GRP-03 proposals were refused and their slots reopened; the IDEA-0013 note said 'long lens', but that film is macro and locked wides. Still unverified: the dome's visibility from the terrace today (sources disagree, see research_note), which is a drop_if; the 1990 book; access. The strongest remaining objection: the payoff frame is centred on the hill where the man named in beat 1 has his resting place; nothing in the voice refers to it, but a viewer who knows the garden will read the held frame that way.

suggested_location.name: Lunuganga, Geoffrey Bawa's country garden on the Dedduwa Lake, Bentota: the approach from the southern gateway up the drive and steps to the entrance terrace, and the Cinnamon Hill vista south to the white dagoba of the Katakuliya temple across the lake

also_known_as.name: Lunuganga
also_known_as.meaning: 'salt river' in Sinhala, as the Geoffrey Bawa Trust translates it

also_known_as.name: Lunuganga Estate
also_known_as.meaning: the name under which the garden, tours and guest rooms are presented today

suggested_location.region: Galle District, Southern Province, on the Dedduwa Lake a mile inland of the south-west coast, in the Bentota Divisional Secretariat. OpenStreetMap/Nominatim places the estate (6.4039, 80.0217) in Galle District; Wikipedia's article gives Western Province, which is wrong: the estate lies south of the Bentota Ganga, which divides Galle from Kalutara District, and the biographer's route to it crosses the river going south before turning inland. The Katakuliya temple across the lake could not be located in OpenStreetMap; it is filmed only from inside the garden. District count: Galle 4 on the slate without GRP-02/03 (IDEA-0123, 0140, 0145, 0183), moves to 5. (The GRP-03 lake-island proposal for IDEA-0036, which would have made it 6, was refused and the slot reopened.)
suggested_location.why_here: Because this is the one place where the distinction C021 draws, between the wish to take up an object and the sticking to it, is written into a documented history rather than read into a landscape. The garden's biographer records, in the same account, attempts to buy neighbouring land that the owners refused and, instead, a loggia built to frame a view of the land that was not sold; and the garden's principal vista, cleared over the 1950s and completed after 1958, ends on the white dagoba of a temple across the lake that the garden has never owned. Acts of having and acts of viewing sit side by side in the record, and the record gives none of the minds, which is exactly what the texts say a camera cannot see. And the place is one of the most cinematic gardens in Asia: a designed blind approach through shade and a sudden reveal onto a long composed view over water, which a single walking take can film without adding anything.

historical_thread.story: Lunuganga ('salt river') is an estate of about twenty-five acres on a promontory in the Dedduwa Lake, a brackish lagoon fed by an estuary of the Bentota Ganga, about a mile inland of the sea. In the biographer's words it had been a Dutch cinnamon garden and a British rubber estate, and 'in 1948 there was nothing more here than an undistinguished bungalow surrounded by 25 acres of rubber trees, enjoying only limited views northwards across the Dedduwa Lake'. Geoffrey Bawa (1919-2003), then a lawyer and later the island's best-known architect, acquired it in 1948 or 1949 and worked on it until his death in 2003. His biographer David Robson, in Geoffrey Bawa: The Complete Works (2002, pages 238-260, reproduced on Archnet), gives the only continuous account reached: 'since then hills have been moved, terraces cut, woods replanted, new vistas opened up and the old estate road has been buried within a ha-ha'; in the early 1950s Bawa 'levelled the northern terrace and began clearing the Cinnamon Hill vista'; work stopped when he left to study architecture in Britain in 1953, and 'after 1958 the Cinnamon Hill vista was completed'. Robson quotes an eyewitness, the Danish architect Ulrik Plesner, writing for a Danish magazine in 1959 (quoted from Brian Brace Taylor's 1986 monograph, p. 44): 'whilst the hill was being excavated ... suddenly it was realized that there was a hidden view lying behind 200 metres of trees and plants. The chairs were turned, all other work was abandoned, and in a few hours trees were felled, undergrowth removed, branches cut, snakes killed and a whole new view - and garden - was made.' Plesner does not say which view this was. Robson then records: 'Over the years Bawa was unsuccessful in his attempts to extend the estate by acquiring the lower half of the promontory on which it was set, but he did manage to acquire two neighbouring islands', one of which, he says, was registered as a wildlife sanctuary in the 1970s after the land-ceiling legislation; and, of the 1980s, that Bawa 'still had ambitions to buy out his neighbour and extend his domain westwards beyond the "Field of Jars" but the owner could not be budged. And so Bawa built a new pool court and loggia on the west side of his bedroom, framing the view towards his neighbour's land.' Of the main view Robson writes that it runs south from the entrance terrace through a corridor of trees to 'a lone moonamal tree [that] leans over a large pot on the summit of Cinnamon Hill, pointing to the white dagoba of the distant Buddhist temple beyond a thin sliver of water', and that the Katakuliya temple 'with its white stupa, forms the focus of the Cinnamon Hill vista'. He tells, undated and unsourced, that the temple's priest suggested a donation to repaint the stupa, and that Bawa offered half the cost since only half of it could be seen from the garden. The Geoffrey Bawa Trust's site quotes Bawa: 'The area one was dealing with was about twenty-five acres but with its surrounding lakes the land beyond seems to go on forever.' Robson also wrote that if the garden were ignored 'for a week the paths and staircases will clog up with leaves; ... for a month the lawns will run wild; ... for a year the terraces will start to crumble; after two or three years the jungle will return'. After Bawa's death the estate passed to a trust; the gardens are open on guided tours and part of the estate takes overnight guests.
historical_thread.how_it_binds: C021's decisive sentence is that desire-to-act is the wish to take up the object and not the force that makes the mind stick to it; the sticking is greed [C021-P:L69], and the wish to do is 'a wanting without sticking' that goes with greed in a greedy mind and against it in a mind opposed to greed [C021-M:L27]. The garden's record holds the two things that sentence separates, as documented acts on the same ground: attempts to acquire land, which did not succeed, and the making of views onto land, water and a temple that were never acquired, including a loggia built to face the very land that was not sold, and a principal vista whose end point belongs to a temple across the lake. A view is the clearest case the island offers of an object that can be taken up and cannot be possessed. The binding is not that the garden 'resembles' the doctrine; it is that the documented history poses the doctrine's own question (is the wanting here the wish to do, or the sticking?) and cannot answer it, because a record of acts carries no minds, which is the same limit the series puts on its camera. C032 binds through the object: feeling is the tasting of an object's flavour and arises with every mind that takes an object [C032-P:L43]; the gladness is mental and is counted in both greed-rooted and wholesome minds [C032-M:L9]. The view gives an object to taste without anything to own.
what_is_certain: The estate lies in Galle District (OpenStreetMap/Nominatim reverse geocode of 6.4039, 80.0217; the Bentota Divisional Secretariat is in Galle District), south of the Bentota Ganga. Wikipedia's 'Western Province' is wrong.
It was a cinnamon garden in the Dutch period and a rubber estate in the British (Robson 2002; Wikipedia agrees).
Geoffrey Bawa (1919-2003) held the estate from the late 1940s until his death in 2003 and worked on the garden throughout; Robson (2002) calls it 'more than half a century'.

The biographer's account (Robson 2002, pp. 238-260) says the Cinnamon Hill vista was begun in the early 1950s and completed after 1958, that hills were moved and the old estate road buried in a ha-ha, and that the principal view from the entrance terrace ends on the white dagoba of the Katakuliya temple across the water.

The same account records unsuccessful attempts to acquire the lower half of the promontory, the acquisition of two neighbouring islands, a later refusal by the western neighbour to sell, and the building of a pool court and loggia framing the view towards that neighbour's land.

Ulrik Plesner's 1959 account of a hidden view found behind 200 metres of trees and cleared in a few hours is quoted by Robson from Taylor (1986, p. 44), who took it from Plesner's Danish magazine article.

The Geoffrey Bawa Trust quotes Bawa's sentence about twenty-five acres and the land beyond seeming to go on forever; the trust runs guided garden tours (currently at 11:00, 14:00 and 15:00) and overnight stays.
what_is_disputed: The year of acquisition: 1948 (Robson 2002; the Geoffrey Bawa Trust: 'purchased the property in 1948') against 1949 (Wikipedia, which says the bungalow was let to the local tax collector in 1948 and bought by Bawa in 1949). Kept as two years; not averaged.

The lowered hill. One garden-history blog (2022, drawing on Robson and Sansoni's garden monograph and on a 2010 Hortus article) says three metres were removed from a hilltop to open a glimpse of water and hills topped by a white stupa; another (2017) says the three metres were removed so the view down to the lake would not be interrupted. Robson (2002) says only that 'hills have been moved'. Neither version could be checked against a primary, so the film does not use the figure or its purpose.
The proposal's 'lane sunk so as not to interrupt the view': Robson says the old estate road was buried within a ha-ha, and does not tie it to the temple view.
Which view Plesner's 1959 account describes: he does not say, and the film does not identify it with the temple vista.

The repainting anecdote (the temple's priest asks for a donation to repaint the stupa; half the cost is offered because only half can be seen): told by Robson without date or source, evidently from Bawa's own circle, which had the most to gain from its wit. Recorded here; not used in the film (see risks).

The wildlife-sanctuary registration of the larger island in the 1970s, which Robson gives with a motive ('to prevent its being confiscated'); not confirmed from any register, and kept out of the film because it gives a motive and enters land-reform politics.

The trust's name: 'the Lunuganga Trust' in Robson (2002) and Wikipedia, 'the Geoffrey Bawa Trust' on the current site. The current relation between the trust and the hotel operator was not established and is not entered.

Whether the dome is still visible from the terrace today at the size Robson describes (his account is from 2002; a recent Commons photograph of the vista, taken from an unknown point on the lawn, does not resolve it at thumbnail size).

what_to_film: The single take, walked on several mornings so that one complete take is clean: from the laterite track at the overgrown southern gateway, up the steep drive under the trees, to the foot of the steps, up the steps, onto the entrance terrace, the turn, and the stop. Stabilised, eye height, 35 mm, no zoom, no cut.

The hold on the Cinnamon Hill vista from the entrance terrace for at least ninety seconds, as the low morning sun moves onto the side of the dagoba; the frame composed so the dome reads as a small white point, not enlarged.
Live sound throughout: footsteps on laterite and stone, birds, leaves, the lake; any sweeping or cutting heard, not staged.
Before the shoot, a scout from the terrace with a long lens to confirm the dagoba is still visible along the vista (for checking only; that footage is not used in the film).

Not filmed: the temple itself at any distance closer than the garden's own view; the bungalow interior; the guest rooms and the western loggia; the top of the hill in the middle of the vista at close range; any guest, visitor or identifiable staff member.
suggested_location.access: A private estate held by a trust and open to paying visitors on scheduled guided tours (currently 11:00, 14:00 and 15:00 per the trust's site), with overnight guest accommodation. An early-morning continuous take of the approach and the entrance terrace needs the trust's written permission and cooperation to keep the terrace clear of guests and staff for the length of the take; this has not been asked or confirmed. Reached by road from the coast road at Bentota, crossing the causeway at the neck between the river and the lake; the final approach, per Robson, is by a laterite track through paddy to the southern gateway. No drone is planned; none would be flown over a working guest estate without separate permission and Civil Aviation clearance.
suggested_location.best_time: December to March, the drier months on this coast before the south-west monsoon (roughly May to September), on a clear morning, ideally after overnight rain for clean air on the far shore; the take between about 06:30 and 08:30, when the drive is still in shade, the dome takes low side light from the east, and no public tour is on the grounds. Several consecutive mornings should be booked.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, 2026-09-26; nothing checked on the ground. The principal source is David Robson's Geoffrey Bawa: The Complete Works (2002), pp. 238-260, read in full as reproduced on Archnet (through a Wayback Machine capture; the live Archnet site returned a bot check). Robson was Bawa's friend and biographer and published this while Bawa was alive; his account is the best reached but is not neutral, and he notes himself that Bawa kept no systematic record, so the chronology is reconstructed. The primary book, Lunuganga (Bawa, Bon and Sansoni, 1990), and Robson and Sansoni's later garden monograph were not reached; Plesner's 1959 article and Taylor's 1986 monograph were reached only as quoted by Robson. The proposal's key facts were checked and corrected: the district (Galle, not Western Province), the acquisition year (1948 or 1949, both kept), the length of the work (more than half a century, not forty years), the lowered hill and sunk lane (not in Robson; the three-metre figure is in later garden writing, told two ways), and the temple anecdote (Robson's, with a donation request that is kept out of the voice). The district was verified by reverse geocoding and against the Divisional Secretariat. Galle moves from 4 to 5, within the preferred range (the GRP-03 lake-island proposal that would have made it 6 was refused). The temple across the lake could not be located on OpenStreetMap and was deliberately not researched further, because the film never goes to it. Images: five Commons files, each confirmed by the imageinfo API and viewed; none shows the dome clearly. The Commons description of the Cinnamon Hill file describes the hill as the maker's resting place; that description is not repeated in the caption and the film does not use it. Access, permissions, the current visibility of the dome from the terrace and the current state of the approach are unverified. Audit 2026-09-26: Robson's text on Archnet was re-read against every quotation in the voice and the thread; all hold. Current visibility of the dome remains unresolved: a 2019 visitor account says the hill and pot draw the eye 'towards the top of the hill, the lake and the temple', and a guest listing says the Cinnamon Hill House vistas 'rest on a distant Buddhist stupa', while one web summary (source not traced) says the temple is now hidden by trees. The Commons description of the Cinnamon Hill photograph calls the hill Bawa's 'final resting place', which confirms that the payoff frame is composed on it.

unknowns: No access, permission or filming condition has been asked for or confirmed. Everything here is a research direction.
Whether the dagoba is still visible from the entrance terrace today, and at what size in a 35 mm frame.
Whether the approach Robson describes (laterite track, southern gateway, steep drive, steps to the entrance terrace) is still the approach in use, or whether guests and tours now arrive another way.
The text of the 1990 book, including the maker's own account of the main vista and of any earthworks for it; Plesner's 1959 article; Taylor's 1986 monograph.
The dates of the failed attempts to buy the lower promontory and the western land, and of the western loggia.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location was proposed by Claude and awaits Chathura's review; it has not been confirmed. The garden's history is documentary at one remove: a biographer's account published in 2002 during the subject's lifetime, which quotes a 1959 eyewitness through a 1986 monograph, supplemented by the trust's own site and by later garden writing where they disagree. The district was checked by reverse geocoding and against the Divisional Secretariat. Access, permissions and filming conditions are desk research and unverified. No scene or shot has been filmed.
